items.prompt: A shooting star is not actually a star falling from the sky. What is really producing that streak of light?

options.label: A star running out of fuel and dropping
options.feedback: A true star is unimaginably larger than anything crossing our sky in a second, and none has ever been seen to fall — what falls is something tiny and near, not a star at all.

options.label: A small bit of rock or dust burning up as it plunges into the atmosphere
options.feedback: Something no bigger than a pebble or a grain of sand, moving at tremendous speed, is enough to light up a streak that outshines every real star nearby.

options.label: Sunlight reflecting off a passing cloud of ice
options.feedback: The streak appears in the middle of the night, in clear dark sky, with no cloud or sunlight involved at all.

options.label: Lightning discharging at very high altitude
options.feedback: A shooting star crosses the sky in a smooth, single streak, quite unlike the branching, jagged flash of a lightning bolt, and it happens in perfectly clear weather.

items.ok_line: A whole streak of light, from a speck too small to ever see in daylight.
items.ko_line: The light comes from something tiny and close to Earth, not from anything as vast and distant as an actual star.
items.exp_title: A speck of rock, not a star
items.exp_text: What produces a shooting star is usually a fragment of rock or dust no larger than a grain of sand or a small pebble, left drifting through space long before it ever reaches Earth. When that fragment meets the top of the atmosphere it is moving many kilometres every second, and at that speed it is destroyed within a second or two, releasing enough light in the process to outshine every true star around it. The streak you see is that brief destruction, not the star it is named after.

items.prompt: Why does a meteor glow so brightly rather than simply heating up quietly as it enters the atmosphere?

options.label: Air is compressed and heated so violently ahead of it that the air and its surface both glow
options.feedback: Moving that fast, the meteoroid has no time to push air gently aside — it slams into it, and the crushed air ahead becomes hot enough to glow on its own.

options.label: It is struck by cosmic radiation as it enters the atmosphere
options.feedback: There is no burst of radiation striking a meteoroid at that moment. The light is produced by the meteoroid's own violent passage through the air, nothing external.

options.label: It reflects the light of the Moon and stars
options.feedback: A speck this small reflecting starlight would be utterly invisible. What is seen is far too bright to be a reflection of anything.

options.label: Friction slowly warms it the way rubbing your hands together does
options.feedback: Ordinary rubbing warms things gradually over seconds. This glow appears and vanishes within a single second, driven by something far more violent than gentle friction.

items.ok_line: It is not the meteoroid quietly warming up — it is the air ahead of it being crushed into a glow.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to the air directly in the path of something moving many kilometres every second, rather than what happens to the object itself.
items.exp_text: A meteoroid enters the atmosphere so fast that the air directly ahead of it has no time to flow smoothly out of the way, and instead gets violently compressed into a cushion of shocked, superheated air. That cushion becomes hot enough to glow brightly on its own, and it in turn heats and vaporises the surface of the meteoroid itself, adding a glowing trail of vaporised material behind it. The bright streak is this compressed, glowing air and vapour, not a slow warming of the object by rubbing against the atmosphere.

items.prompt: Why does the flash of a typical shooting star last only about a second, rather than continuing for much longer?

options.label: The atmosphere quickly extinguishes any glow
options.feedback: The compressed, glowing air keeps forming for as long as the object keeps moving fast through it. It is not the atmosphere snuffing the glow out early.

options.label: Earth's rotation carries the meteor out of view
options.feedback: The meteoroid is moving vastly faster than the ground beneath it turns, so Earth's rotation over a single second makes no meaningful difference to what is seen.

options.label: The meteoroid changes direction and leaves the atmosphere again
options.feedback: A typical meteoroid does not survive its plunge to head back out to space. It is consumed on the way down, not deflected away.

options.label: The tiny meteoroid is entirely vaporised within that time
options.feedback: Something the size of a pebble or grain of sand simply does not have enough material left to keep glowing once it has all boiled away.

items.ok_line: The flash ends because there is nothing left of the object to keep it burning.
items.ko_line: Think about how much material a speck the size of a grain of sand actually has to offer, once it starts vaporising that fast.
items.exp_title: Burning through in a single second
items.exp_text: A typical meteoroid carries only a tiny amount of material, and the extreme heat generated by its plunge through the thick lower atmosphere vaporises that material very quickly. Once every part of it has boiled away, there is nothing left to sustain the glowing cushion of compressed air or the trail of vapour behind it, and the light stops. For an object that small, that whole process is usually finished within about a second of it first becoming visible.

items.prompt: Shooting stars from anywhere on Earth tend to appear at roughly the same altitude, high above the ground. Why does the glow consistently start and end in that same narrow band of the atmosphere?

options.label: Meteoroids are all made of exactly the same material
options.feedback: Meteoroids vary quite a bit in what they are made of, from stony material to metal. That variety does not stop them from all beginning to glow at roughly the same height.

options.label: Satellites orbiting at that height knock them into view
options.feedback: No satellite needs to be involved for a meteor to appear, and this happens even where no satellite is anywhere nearby.

options.label: That is where the air first becomes dense enough to compress and heat violently in front of the object
options.feedback: Below that height the air is too thick for a meteoroid to survive long, and above it the air is too thin to compress hard enough to produce a bright glow — so the glow reliably begins and ends in the narrow band between.

options.label: Earth's magnetic field is strongest at that height
options.feedback: A meteoroid is not electrically charged in a way that would make the magnetic field relevant here. The height is set by the thickness of the air, not by magnetism.

items.ok_line: One band of altitude is where the air is thick enough to matter but thin enough to still let the object through.
items.ko_line: The object is travelling down through air that keeps getting denser. Ask at what point that increasing density first becomes able to crush and heat it violently.
items.exp_title: The one altitude where the air first bites
items.exp_text: High above the ground the atmosphere is far too thin to compress meaningfully in front of a fast-moving object, so nothing glows there. Lower down, roughly eighty to a hundred kilometres up, the air first becomes dense enough for that violent compression and heating to begin, which is why the streak reliably starts around there. A typical meteoroid is usually destroyed within that same narrow band, before it can descend into the still thicker air below, which is why the glow so consistently ends at roughly the same height as well.

items.prompt: Why do meteor showers return on roughly the same calendar dates year after year?

options.label: Earth's orbit crosses the same trail of debris at the same point every year
options.feedback: A comet leaves a trail of dust and small rock scattered along its own orbit, and Earth's orbit around the Sun brings it back through that same trail at essentially the same point each year.

options.label: The Sun releases a burst of debris on a yearly cycle
options.feedback: The debris does not come freshly from the Sun each year. It is old material, scattered long ago, sitting in a fixed trail that Earth simply passes through again on its own orbit.

options.label: Meteoroids drift into Earth's path only once a year
options.feedback: The debris in a meteor shower's trail sits there constantly, all year round. It is Earth's own position, not the debris drifting in, that changes with the calendar.

options.label: Cold winter or summer air makes meteors easier to see on those dates
options.feedback: Showers occur at fixed dates regardless of season, appearing in every month of the year at their own particular time — the weather does not decide when a shower happens.

items.ok_line: The debris trail never moves. Earth simply drives back through the same stretch of it every year.
items.ko_line: Think about which is fixed in place year after year, and which is the thing doing the repeated travelling.
items.exp_title: Driving through the same trail again
items.exp_text: A comet sheds a stream of dust and small fragments as it swings through the inner solar system, and that stream stays scattered along the comet's own orbital path for a very long time afterward. Earth's own orbit around the Sun crosses that same path at essentially the same point in its yearly journey, so Earth ploughs through the densest part of the trail again at almost the same time on the calendar every year. The extra meteors of a shower are simply Earth driving back through debris that has been sitting there all along.

items.prompt: During a meteor shower, why do all the individual streaks appear to radiate outward from one single point in the sky?

options.label: The debris particles collide and scatter from a central spot
options.feedback: The particles are far too thinly scattered to collide with one another in any meaningful way. There is no central collision point sending them outward.

options.label: The particles travel on nearly parallel paths, which appear to converge to a point from your perspective
options.feedback: The same way distant railway tracks running side by side appear to meet at a point on the horizon, meteors travelling on parallel paths appear to stream outward from one shared point when seen from within that stream.

options.label: Earth's gravity pulls every particle toward the same spot
options.feedback: Gravity pulls each particle toward the centre of the Earth, not toward one particular point on the dome of the sky as seen from any one observer.

options.label: They are all reflections of a single bright meteor
options.feedback: Each streak is its own separate object burning up, not a copy or reflection of one original flash.

items.ok_line: It is a trick of perspective, the same one that makes parallel lines seem to meet in the distance.
items.ko_line: The particles in a shower are all moving on very similar, nearly parallel paths. Think about how parallel lines look when you view them end-on.
items.exp_title: Parallel paths meeting at a point
items.exp_text: All the fragments in a single meteor shower are remnants of the same debris trail, moving through space on paths that are very nearly parallel to one another. Viewed from the ground, a set of parallel paths does not look parallel at all — much as two straight railway tracks seem to converge to a single point far in the distance, parallel meteor trails all appear to stretch back toward one shared point in the sky. That apparent point of origin is simply where the perspective lines up, not a place where anything is actually happening.

items.prompt: Why are meteors generally easier to spot after midnight than in the hours right after sunset?

options.label: The sky is simply darker after midnight
options.feedback: By a few hours after sunset the sky is already just as dark as it will be at any later hour, so darkness alone does not explain the difference.

options.label: Meteoroids are attracted to the Moon's position after midnight
options.feedback: The extra meteors appear whether or not the Moon is anywhere near the sky at the time, so its position is not what is responsible.

options.label: After midnight your location faces into the direction Earth is travelling in its orbit
options.feedback: Facing forward into Earth's own motion, you meet debris head-on, adding the speed of Earth's travel to the speed of impact and sweeping up more of it — much like a moving car's windscreen catching more insects than its rear window.

options.label: Meteoroids only enter the atmosphere after midnight
options.feedback: Debris is present in Earth's path at every hour. What changes after midnight is which side of Earth is facing into that debris, not whether the debris is there at all.

items.ok_line: After midnight, you are standing on the side of Earth sweeping forward into the debris, not trailing behind it.
items.ko_line: Earth itself is moving forward along its orbit. Think about which side of a moving object meets oncoming material head-on, and which side only catches material that catches up to it.
items.exp_title: The windscreen side of a moving Earth
items.exp_text: Earth travels forward along its orbit around the Sun, and at any given moment one side of the planet faces into that direction of travel while the opposite side trails behind it. After local midnight, your position has rotated around to the leading, forward-facing side, so debris in Earth's path strikes there almost head-on, adding Earth's own orbital speed to the impact and sweeping up more of it. Before midnight you are still on the trailing side, catching only the debris that happens to be moving fast enough to catch up with Earth from behind.

items.prompt: Why does an unusually bright meteor, a fireball, sometimes leave a glowing trail hanging in the sky for a minute or more after the flash itself has faded?

options.label: A large enough meteoroid vaporises enough hot, glowing material to leave a lingering trail as it drifts and cools
options.feedback: A bigger source produces a genuine cloud of hot vapour and ionised air, and that cloud takes real time to drift, spread, and cool before it stops glowing.

options.label: The Moon lights up the smoke afterward
options.feedback: The lingering trail is seen on moonless nights just as often, glowing under its own remaining heat rather than reflecting any other light.

options.label: The observer's eyes retain an afterimage of the flash
options.feedback: An eye's afterimage fades within a few seconds at most and looks the same to every observer regardless of where they stand — this trail is a real object in the sky that drifts and changes shape over minutes, visible from many places at once.

options.label: It is an unrelated cloud that happened to be there already
options.feedback: The trail appears exactly along the path the fireball just travelled and is absent moments before the flash, so it cannot be a cloud that was already sitting there.

items.ok_line: A big enough meteoroid leaves behind a real, physical cloud of glowing debris, not just an impression.
items.ko_line: A very bright fireball vaporises far more material than an ordinary faint meteor. Think about what becomes of all that extra vaporised material once the flash itself is over.
items.exp_title: A cloud left behind by a bigger burn
items.exp_text: An unusually bright fireball is typically a larger meteoroid, and destroying more material releases far more hot, glowing vapour and ionised air than an ordinary faint meteor does. Rather than dispersing instantly, this larger cloud lingers along the meteor's path, catching high-altitude winds that stretch and twist it into changing shapes while it slowly cools and fades. The brighter the original flash, the more material was vaporised to produce it, and the longer the resulting trail tends to remain visible.

items.prompt: Why do some meteors flash green, orange, or violet rather than plain white?

options.label: The colour depends only on how fast the meteor is travelling
options.feedback: Speed affects how bright a meteor is, but the particular colour it flashes comes from something else entirely, not from speed alone.

options.label: Coloured meteors are actually reflections off distant city lights
options.feedback: Brightly coloured meteors are seen just as often over open ocean and remote wilderness, far from any city light to reflect.

options.label: The atmosphere itself changes colour at different heights
options.feedback: The atmosphere is the same transparent gas at every height a meteor passes through. It is not the air that supplies the colour.

options.label: Different elements in the meteoroid and surrounding air glow with their own characteristic colours when heated that intensely
options.feedback: Just as different elements burned in a flame each give off their own particular colour, elements such as magnesium or sodium in a vaporising meteoroid glow with their own distinct hue.

items.ok_line: Each colour is a fingerprint of which element is glowing at that instant.
items.ko_line: Think about what is actually being vaporised and heated during the flash, and whether different substances might glow with their own particular colours when that hot.
items.exp_title: The colour of a particular element burning
items.exp_text: A meteoroid is not pure rock but a mix of different elements, and the surrounding air it compresses and heats contributes its own elements too. Heated intensely enough to glow, each particular element tends to release light of its own characteristic colour — magnesium commonly glowing green, sodium glowing orange, and other elements contributing violet or blue. The exact mix of colour in a given flash depends on which elements happen to be present and vaporising in that meteoroid at that moment.

items.prompt: Why does the flash of a meteor sometimes end with a sudden bright flare rather than simply dimming out smoothly?

options.label: It briefly leaves the atmosphere before falling back in
options.feedback: A meteoroid this deep into the atmosphere has already lost too much speed and material to climb back out to space. It does not exit and re-enter.

options.label: The meteoroid suddenly breaks apart under the stress of compression and heating, exposing fresh surface all at once
options.feedback: Shattering into several pieces at once exposes a burst of fresh, unvaporised surface to the same violent heat all together, producing a brief, much brighter flare before what remains finishes burning.

options.label: It passes briefly through a patch of denser air
options.feedback: The atmosphere thickens gradually and smoothly with decreasing altitude. There is no sudden patch of denser air to cause an abrupt flare.

options.label: The camera or eye watching it briefly overexposes
options.feedback: The same sudden brightening is recorded independently by observers and cameras in different locations at once, so it is a real event in the sky, not an artefact of any single observer.

items.ok_line: A sudden burst of fresh surface, all exposed to the heat at once, briefly outshines the steady burn that came before it.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to the surface being burned away if the object itself suddenly shatters into several pieces mid-flight.
items.exp_title: A last burst of fresh surface
items.exp_text: As a meteoroid plunges deeper into the thickening atmosphere, the mounting pressure and heat can shatter it into several fragments in an instant, an event called fragmentation. Each fragment exposes surface material that had not yet been vaporised, and all of that fresh material burns at once, producing a much brighter flare than the steady glow that came before it. What remains of the pieces then finishes burning far more quickly, since there is far less material left in each one.
